title: The daughter of the fire
hookLine: a king's fire offering gives him a son and a daughter: why Hindus still make offerings into fire
carry: yajna, offer to the fire, and blessing returns

cards: A king has a fire lit because he wants a son. Drupada of Panchala has been humbled by Drona, and he wants someone who can answer that. Priests perform a great sacrifice.

From the fire a young man rises, armed and shining: Dhrishtadyumna. Then, from the middle of the altar, a young woman. Dark, the text says, with eyes like lotus petals, and the scent of blue lotus around her.
The sacrifice was for a son. The fire gives a daughter too.

teach.b: As she rises, the text says, a voice is heard from the sky: this dark girl will bring about the destruction of the warrior class.
She's named Krishnaa, the dark one, and Draupadi, Drupada's daughter, and Panchali, the princess of Panchala. Hindus also call her Yajnaseni: the one born from the sacrifice.
That sacrifice is a yajna, one of Hinduism's oldest practices. Offerings of ghee and grain are poured into a sacred fire, and Agni, the fire god, carries them up to the gods.

teach.h: NOURISH THE GODS, AND BE NOURISHED.
teach.b: In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna puts the idea simply: nourish the gods with your offering, and the gods will nourish you; caring for each other, both reach the highest good. Drupada's yajna is that exchange made dramatic.
He offers into the fire, and the fire gives back two children. Hindus still do this on a smaller scale.
A havan, a home fire offering, is lit for a new house, a wedding, a fresh start, with the family tossing in ghee and grain while the priest says svaha.
The same old shape: something given away in fire, and blessing hoped for in return.

teach.h: THE PANDAVAS SET OUT FOR PANCHALA.
teach.b: Back in the story, the Pandavas, still hiding as brahmins in a town, hear it all from a traveling brahmin: the fire, the brother and sister, and the swayamvara Drupada has announced, a princess's own choosing of a husband among gathered suitors.
Kunti sees her sons grow restless, the text says, and says it's time to go to Panchala. So they set out, still dressed as brahmins.

how: Draupadi is honored as a goddess in parts of South India: some villages in Tamil Nadu keep temples to Draupadi Amman and hold festivals in her name, some with firewalking.

games.q: a friend at a havan asks why you'd throw good ghee and rice into a fire. by today's story, what fits?
o: it's an offering: Agni carries it to the gods, and blessing comes back, like Drupada's fire gave him children.
it's to make the fire burn hotter and look good.
it's a way of using up old food before a new start.
games.why: in a yajna nothing is just wasted. it's given, and the Gita calls it an exchange: nourish the gods, and they nourish you.

practice: If you have a diya or a candle you can safely light, light a small flame; if not, picture one. Many Hindus light a lamp at their home shrine every day, the simplest offering of fire.
Hold something small in your mind to give: a worry, a thank-you, an hour of your day. If you pray, offer it into the flame the way a havan offering goes in, with svaha.
If you don't, just let it go into the light, and notice what comes back: a little warmth, a little calm.

wordCard.voice: Draupadi's swayamvara. The choosing of a husband for the princess born from the fire: Krishnaa, Draupadi, Panchali.

orig.note: Sanskrit yajña: sacrifice, an offering into sacred fire; Draupadi is called Yajnaseni, born from one.

carryVoice: Your line: yajna, offer to the fire, and blessing returns. Drupada's fire gave him two children. Tomorrow, the bow.
